A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AudioTrust and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and extensive appendices. Their matching tasks and experiments support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of 14 audio models, including quantitative benchmark results and appendix comparisons involving prompts, modalities, and acoustic interference.

after.justification: v4 retains these original experiments and adds results from Qwen3-based evaluation in Tables 2–6.

M1.justification: The modular inference/evaluation architecture in Appendix C and the benchmark construction procedures remain unchanged. Additional judging changes evaluation protocols; newly specified PGD details do not establish a changed attack-generation method.

E1.justification: The same fairness scenarios, hallucination categories, safety domains, privacy tasks, acoustic interference conditions, and authentication tasks remain. BigBenchAudio was already used in v3 Appendix H.2; the new dataset summaries do not establish additional task or population coverage.

E2.justification: Both versions evaluate the same nine open-source and five closed-source audio models and retain the corresponding text-only comparisons. Qwen3 is added as an evaluator of responses, rather than as another benchmarked competitor.

E3.justification: v4 adds Qwen3 judging across five dimensions, changes unfairness to fairness scoring and FAR to impostor rejection rate, and removes HRR. These substantially revise evaluation scoring without establishing model reruns. New Table 32 reports 82 samples for five robustness categories, conflicting with the retained 40-sample statement in H.3.1; actual sample-size changes remain unresolved.

E4.justification: Paired GPT-4o/Qwen3 results in Tables 2–6 introduce broad evidence about sensitivity to evaluator choice. For example, Step-Audio2 receives physical-violation scores of 2.76 and 8.39 respectively. Appendix G.2 also newly reports manual checks of synthesized privacy audio. Existing modality, emotion, gender, background-audio, and prompt-strength analyses remain.

E5.justification: No new repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. The Monte Carlo statement in D.3 and human-validation sampling and agreement figures in C remain unchanged. Table subscripts represent differences from averages, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 2–6 add extensive Qwen3 results, and several existing reported values change. Table 4's GPT-4o aggregate inference-refusal rate changes from 7.41% to 9.02%. Qwen2.5-Omni's identity-bypass result changes from 36% FAR to 19% IRR, beyond a simple complement conversion. These are reporting and evaluation changes, not established same-setting model improvements.

T1.justification: Equation 1 in D.3 changes the normalized signed group-probability difference to one minus that difference. F.4 removes the HRR definition, and I.4 replaces false acceptance with correct impostor rejection. These are limited mathematical-definition changes; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: a comprehensive audio-specific trustworthiness benchmark spanning six dimensions, 26 subtasks, and 14 models. The principal claims about acoustic vulnerabilities and deployment risks retain their scope.

C2.justification: Appendix B adds extensive model-specific mechanism and tradeoff interpretations, and new Appendix L recommends training interventions across all six dimensions. Section 5 expands the rationale for treating demographic inference as privacy leakage, and K adds a speech-rate limitation. Section 7 changes its interpretation from paralinguistic cues aiding authentication attacks to having limited influence.

D1.justification: H.2 newly specifies PGD, an L-infinity constraint, an 8 × 2^-15 perturbation budget, and 30–40 steps. Appendices N–O add provenance, licensing, and dataset summaries. Access documentation also changes: the explicit Hugging Face dataset link is replaced by a post-acceptance release promise, and repository pointers are revised.

R1.justification: v4 adds references supporting privacy profiling, fairness-aware alignment, and Qwen3 evaluation. It replaces the mismatched autonomous-driving SafeBench citation with the multimodal SafeBench work. Most other reference changes update publication metadata; the paper's overall research positioning remains stable.

P1.justification: The core section order and most existing prose remain. Changes include expanded model descriptions, localized explanatory and terminology revisions, new lessons and dataset-statistics appendices, acknowledgments, and author, affiliation, and conference-header edits.

P2.justification: Tables 2–6 are substantially reformatted to display paired evaluator scores with revised captions and legends. v4 updates the Figure 2 leaderboard, adds 14 model radar charts in Figure 3, and introduces dataset-summary Tables 28–33. Existing conceptual figures are largely retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v4 adds useful evaluator comparisons and concrete attack and provenance documentation. However, the fairness conversion introduces inconsistent definitions and values, including Table 7's 1.200 fairness score, while new Table 32 conflicts with the retained 40-sample protocol. Expanded mechanism claims also lack corresponding causal tests. These evidential gains and reliability problems leave the net overall quality change unclear.
